title: The Abbasid Caliphate
subtitle: 945–1258 · The Age of Sultans, the Sunni Revival and the Mongol Sack

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: A caliph who reigns without ruling, and the soldiers — Buyid, then Seljuk — who rule in his name

entries.label: The caliph as a source of legitimacy
entries.hint: For over two centuries the Abbasid caliph kept his palace, his name in the Friday prayer and on the coinage, and the power to invest a ruler with legitimacy — and almost nothing else. Whoever controlled Baghdad ran the state; the caliph made it lawful.
entries.note: Hanne, 'Putting the Caliph in his Place: Power, Authority, and the Late Abbasid Caliphate' (2007); Kennedy, 'The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates' (2016).

entries.label: The Buyid amirs
entries.hint: The Buyids, a Shia dynasty of Daylamite soldiers from the Caspian mountains, held Iraq and western Iran as 'commander of commanders'. Their court, especially under Adud al-Dawla, was one of the most cultivated of the age — and they were careful to keep the Sunni caliph they could have deposed.
entries.note: Busse, 'Chalif und Grosskönig' (1969); Kraemer, 'Humanism in the Renaissance of Islam' (1986); Donohue, 'The Buwayhid Dynasty in Iraq' (2003).

entries.label: Tughril, Alp Arslan and Malik-Shah
entries.hint: The Seljuk Turks entered Baghdad in 1055, took the new title 'sultan', and made themselves the sword of Sunni Islam. Under Alp Arslan and Malik-Shah, guided by the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, the empire ran from the Aegean to Central Asia — the high point of medieval Turkic power.
entries.note: Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire' (2015); Nizam al-Mulk, 'Siyar al-Muluk / Siyasatnama'.

entries.label: The succession wars and the atabeg states
entries.hint: Malik-Shah's death and Nizam al-Mulk's murder — both in 1092 — began decades of war among Seljuk princes. Real power devolved to the atabegs, the Turkish guardian-generals of those princes, who founded their own dynasties: the Zangids of Mosul and Aleppo, the Bori of Damascus, others.
entries.note: Peacock (2015); the atabeg states (Bosworth, 'The New Islamic Dynasties', 1996).

entries.label: Al-Nasir li-Din Allah rebuilds a state
entries.hint: With the Seljuks gone and no sultan near, al-Nasir spent forty-five years rebuilding an actual Abbasid principality in Iraq: an army, a diplomatic game between the Khwarazm-Shahs and the Ghurids, and a reorganised chivalric brotherhood (futuwwa) with the caliph at its head. The last flare of caliphal power.
entries.note: Hartmann, 'an-Nasir li-Din Allah' (1975); Hanne (2007).

entries.label: Al-Musta'sim and the sack of Baghdad
entries.hint: The last caliph, indecisive and badly advised, refused Hulagu's demand to submit. In February 1258 a Mongol army stormed Baghdad, sacked it for a week, and executed the caliph — rolled in a carpet and trampled, so no royal blood would touch the ground. The 626-year line ended.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir's successor chroniclers; Juvayni and Rashid al-Din on the Mongol side; the casualty figures debated (Boyle, 'The Death of the Last Abbasid Caliph', JSS 1961).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Manzikert, the Crusades and the counter-Crusade, the Assassins, and the Mongol storm

entries.label: Manzikert
entries.hint: Alp Arslan's defeat and capture of the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV was, in itself, not decisive — but the Byzantine civil war that followed left Anatolia undefended, and Turkish nomads poured in and stayed. Manzikert is the reason Anatolia became Turkey.
entries.note: the Byzantine and Arabic and Armenian accounts; Hillenbrand, 'Turkish Myth and Muslim Symbol: The Battle of Manzikert' (2007).

entries.label: The First Crusade and the fall of Jerusalem
entries.hint: A Latin Christian army exploited the wreck of Seljuk unity to take Antioch (1098) and then Jerusalem (1099), massacring much of the population. The Muslim world, split between a Sunni Baghdad, a Shia Cairo and warring Turkish emirs, took nearly fifty years to organise a serious response.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn al-Qalanisi, 'Damascus Chronicle'; Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives' (1999).

entries.label: Hattin and the recovery of Jerusalem
entries.loc: the Horns of Hattin, Galilee; Jerusalem
entries.hint: Zangi's capture of Edessa (1144) and Nur al-Din's leadership prepared the ground; Saladin, having taken Egypt and Syria into one hand, destroyed the crusader field army at Hattin and retook Jerusalem eighty-eight years after its loss. The Frankish states shrank to a coastal strip.
entries.note: Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, 'The Rare and Excellent History of Saladin'; Imad al-Din al-Isfahani; Hillenbrand (1999).

entries.label: Hasan-i Sabbah and the war of the dagger
entries.loc: Alamut, in the Elburz mountains; and across the region
entries.hint: Denied any territory large enough to field an army, the Nizari Ismailis under Hasan-i Sabbah seized mountain fortresses and made political murder a systematic instrument: the vizier Nizam al-Mulk in 1092, and scores of emirs, caliphs and princes over the next century and a half, killed by lone devotees who did not expect to escape.
entries.note: Daftary, 'The Assassin Legends' (1994) and 'The Ismailis' (2007); the Western 'hashish' etymology as a hostile fabrication.

entries.label: The destruction of Khwarazm
entries.loc: Transoxiana and Khurasan — Bukhara, Samarqand, Merv, Nishapur
entries.hint: Provoked by the Khwarazm-Shah's execution of his envoys, Genghis Khan turned the full Mongol army west. Bukhara and Samarqand fell in 1220; Merv, Nishapur and Herat — among the greatest cities of the Islamic world — were destroyed with their populations. The eastern Islamic world never recovered its former weight.
entries.note: Juvayni, 'The History of the World-Conqueror'; Ibn al-Athir's contemporary lament; the casualty figures (debated: Morgan, 'The Mongols', 2nd ed. 2007).

entries.label: The sack of Baghdad
entries.hint: Hulagu, Genghis Khan's grandson, took Baghdad after a short siege, sacked it for days, and had the last caliph killed. Contemporaries put the dead in the hundreds of thousands; the libraries were thrown in the Tigris; the canal system, already failing, was finished off. The institutional caliphate was over.
entries.note: Boyle, 'The Death of the Last Abbasid Caliph', JSS 6 (1961); the check to the Mongols came two years later at Ayn Jalut (1260) — see World.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The theory of the powerless caliph, the sultanate as an institution, and the madrasa as state policy

entries.label: Al-Mawardi writes the constitution of the caliphate
entries.hint: Al-Mawardi's 'Ordinances of Government' set out the classic Sunni theory of the caliphate — its qualifications, its powers, the delegation of authority — at the very moment the caliph had none of them. Its real achievement was to make room in the law for a sultan who held power the caliph had 'delegated'.
entries.note: al-Mawardi, 'al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyya', trans. Wahba (1996); Crone, 'Medieval Islamic Political Thought' (2004), ch. 17.

entries.label: The sultanate and Nizam al-Mulk's manual of rule
entries.hint: Under the Seljuks the division became formal: the caliph is the imam of the faith, the sultan holds the sword and the state. Nizam al-Mulk's 'Book of Government' codified how that state should work — the spy network, the audience for petitions, the management of the iqta army, the danger of women and heretics at court.
entries.note: Nizam al-Mulk, 'Siyar al-Muluk', trans. Darke, 'The Book of Government or Rules for Kings' (1960).

entries.label: The madrasa as an instrument of state
entries.loc: Baghdad (the Nizamiyya); Nishapur; across the Seljuk lands
entries.hint: Nizam al-Mulk founded a network of endowed law colleges — the Nizamiyya madrasas — to train Sunni scholars, staff the courts, and counter Shia and Ismaili teaching. The state was now in the business of producing religious knowledge, and the ulama were increasingly on its payroll.
entries.note: Makdisi, 'The Rise of Colleges: Institutions of Learning in Islam and the West' (1981); the Nizamiyya of Baghdad.

entries.label: The iqta becomes the military-fiscal system
entries.hint: Under the Buyids and Seljuks the assignment of a district's tax revenue to a soldier in place of pay (iqta) became the normal way to maintain an army. It tied the military to the land, weakened the free peasantry and the central treasury together, and set the pattern for later Islamic states.
entries.note: Cahen, 'L'évolution de l'iqta du IXe au XIIIe siècle', Annales ESC (1953); Lambton, 'Landlord and Peasant in Persia' (1953).

entries.label: The waqf — the endowment that built the Islamic city
entries.hint: The pious endowment — property whose income is permanently dedicated to a mosque, a madrasa, a hospital, a fountain, a soup kitchen or a founder's descendants — was the legal engine of urban Islamic life. In this period it became ubiquitous, funding almost every public building and a great deal of private wealth-sheltering.
entries.note: the waqf in Islamic law and society (Hoexter; Kuran, 'The Long Divergence', 2011, on its economic effects).

entries.label: Al-Nasir's futuwwa order
entries.loc: Baghdad; and by charter across the region
entries.hint: The caliph al-Nasir took over the urban young-men's fraternities (futuwwa), had himself initiated as their head, and issued membership to rulers from Anatolia to Egypt. It was an attempt to build a caliph-centred network of loyalty across states he could no longer command — chivalry as foreign policy.
entries.note: Hartmann, 'an-Nasir li-Din Allah' (1975); the futuwwa and its Sufi and guild connections.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Sunni revival, al-Ghazali, the Sufi orders, Ibn Arabi, the Shia move to Najaf, and the Assassins' resurrection

entries.label: The Sunni revival
entries.hint: After a century in which Shia dynasties ruled most of the Islamic world, the Seljuks backed a deliberate reassertion of Sunnism: the madrasa network, an alliance of Ash'ari theology with Shafi'i and Hanafi law, public professions of the Sunni creed, and pressure on Mu'tazilism and Shiism alike.
entries.note: the 'Sunni revival' thesis (Makdisi); its qualification (Ephrat, 'A Learned Society in a Period of Transition', 2000; Peacock 2015).

entries.label: Al-Ghazali — law, theology and Sufism reconciled
entries.hint: The most celebrated jurist of his day, al-Ghazali left his Baghdad chair in a crisis of doubt, wandered for a decade, and wrote the 'Revival of the Religious Sciences' — a synthesis that gave Sufi practice a secure place inside Sunni orthodoxy. His 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' checked the prestige of falsafa in the east for centuries.
entries.note: al-Ghazali, 'Ihya Ulum al-Din', 'al-Munqidh min al-Dalal' ('Deliverance from Error'), 'Tahafut al-Falasifa'; Griffel, 'Al-Ghazali's Philosophical Theology' (2009).

entries.label: The Sufi orders become institutions
entries.hint: Sufism moved from a personal path to a set of organised brotherhoods (tariqas) with a founding master, a chain of authority, a rule of life and a lodge (khanqah) to live in. Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani's Qadiriyya and Ahmad al-Rifa'i's Rifa'iyya, both centred in Iraq, were among the first and largest.
entries.note: Trimingham, 'The Sufi Orders in Islam' (1971); Karamustafa, 'Sufism: The Formative Period' (2007).

entries.label: Ibn Arabi and the unity of being
entries.loc: Anatolia; Damascus (where he died and is buried)
entries.hint: An Andalusi who settled in the Near East, Ibn Arabi produced in the 'Meccan Openings' and the 'Bezels of Wisdom' the most ambitious speculative mysticism in Islam — the doctrine, later called wahdat al-wujud, that all existence is a single reality manifesting the divine names. His influence on later Sufi and philosophical thought was immense and contested.
entries.note: Ibn Arabi, 'al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya', 'Fusus al-Hikam'; Chittick, 'The Sufi Path of Knowledge' (1989); the later 'wujudi' controversy.

entries.label: The Shia academy moves to Najaf
entries.hint: Under Buyid protection the Twelver scholars of Baghdad — al-Mufid, al-Sharif al-Murtada, then al-Tusi — built a rational Shia theology and jurisprudence and completed the four canonical Shia books of hadith. After the Seljuks came and Sunni mobs burned al-Tusi's library, he moved the school to Najaf, by the shrine of Ali, where it has been ever since.
entries.note: al-Tusi's works; Modarressi, 'An Introduction to Shi'i Law' (1984); the 1055–56 Baghdad riots.

entries.label: The Nizari 'Resurrection' at Alamut
entries.hint: In 1164 the Nizari imam at Alamut proclaimed the qiyama — the Resurrection — declaring that the age of the sacred law was over and that his community now lived in the spiritual reality the law had only symbolised. It was one of the most radical religious announcements of the Middle Ages, later softened by his successors.
entries.note: Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007), ch. 6; Hodgson, 'The Order of Assassins' (1955).

entries.label: Ibn al-Jawzi and the Hanbali preachers of Baghdad
entries.hint: The Hanbali school, strongest in Baghdad, produced in Ibn al-Jawzi a phenomenally productive scholar and popular preacher who drew huge crowds, attacked what he saw as Sufi and philosophical error ('The Devil's Deception'), and defended a scripture-first, reason-wary piety against the madrasa establishment.
entries.note: Ibn al-Jawzi, 'Talbis Iblis', 'al-Muntazam' (his chronicle); Swartz's studies; the roots of the later Ibn Taymiyya tradition.

entries.label: The Church of the East reaches the Mongols
entries.loc: Central Asia; the Mongol steppe; China
entries.hint: While the Church of the East contracted in Iraq, it expanded east: whole Turkic peoples of the steppe — the Kerait, the Onggud — were Christian, and Mongol royal women of that faith sat at the centre of the empire that destroyed Baghdad. A Christian network now ran from the Tigris to the Yellow Sea.
entries.note: the Church of the East in Asia (Baumer, 'The Church of the East', 2006); the Mongol-era Christians (the later embassy of Rabban Bar Sauma, 1287).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The four-iwan mosque, the Baghdad painters, Mosul inlaid brass, and the Persian poetic renaissance

entries.label: The four-iwan plan and the Seljuk dome
entries.loc: Isfahan (the Friday Mosque); across Iran and the Jazira
entries.hint: Seljuk builders fixed the plan that Iranian mosques and madrasas kept for a thousand years — a courtyard with a great vaulted hall (iwan) on each of its four sides — and raised over the Isfahan mihrab a brick double-shell dome whose geometry (the work of the vizier Taj al-Mulk) is a landmark of structural design.
entries.note: the Masjid-i Jami of Isfahan (its two Seljuk domes, 1086–88); Blair & Bloom, 'The Art and Architecture of Islam 1250–1800' background; Hillenbrand, 'Islamic Architecture' (1994).

entries.label: The tomb tower and the muqarnas vault
entries.hint: The soaring brick tomb tower of Gunbad-i Qabus (1006), 53 metres of flanged cylinder under a conical cap, opens a great age of Iranian funerary architecture. In the same period the muqarnas — the honeycomb of small niches used to bridge a square room to a round dome — was invented and spread across the Islamic world.
entries.note: Gunbad-i Qabus (UNESCO 2012); the origins of muqarnas (Tabbaa, 'The Transformation of Islamic Art during the Sunni Revival', 2001).

entries.label: The Baghdad school of painting
entries.hint: The first great Arab painting appears in illustrated books of the early 13th century — al-Hariri's 'Assemblies' with their crowded, observed scenes of markets and caravans (al-Wasiti's 1237 copy is the masterpiece), the Dioscorides herbals, the animal fables. It flourished for two generations and was cut off by the Mongol sack.
entries.note: the 1237 Maqamat of al-Hariri (BnF Arabe 5847); Ettinghausen, 'Arab Painting' (1962); Grabar, 'The Illustrations of the Maqamat' (1984).

entries.label: Mosul inlaid brass
entries.hint: Mosul metalworkers brought the inlaying of brass with silver and copper to a peak never matched — ewers, basins, candlesticks and pen-boxes covered in figural scenes, courtly and astrological, worked with jeweller's precision. The Mongol advance drove the masters to Cairo and Damascus, carrying the 'Mosul style' with them.
entries.note: the Blacas ewer (Mosul, 1232, British Museum); Ward, 'Islamic Metalwork' (1993).

entries.label: The ceramic revolution of Kashan
entries.hint: The potters of Kashan perfected a hard white 'stonepaste' body and covered it with overglaze enamel painting (mina'i) and metallic lustre, producing figural bowls, star tiles and mosque mihrabs of extraordinary refinement. The word for tile in Persian, kashi, is simply 'from Kashan'.
entries.note: the Kashan lustre and mina'i wares; Watson, 'Persian Lustre Ware' (1985).

entries.label: The Persian renaissance and the Arabic silver age
entries.loc: Ghazna, Tus, Nishapur; and Aleppo, Ma'arra
entries.hint: Firdawsi completed the 'Shahnama', 50,000 verses of Persian national epic, around 1010; Omar Khayyam, better known then as a mathematician, wrote the quatrains later famous in the West. In Arabic, al-Mutanabbi at the Hamdanid court of Aleppo was hailed as the greatest of all poets, and the blind al-Ma'arri of Ma'arra wrote verse of unflinching pessimism and doubt.
entries.note: Firdawsi, 'Shahnama'; al-Mutanabbi's Diwan; al-Ma'arri, 'Luzum ma la yalzam' and 'Risalat al-Ghufran'.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ibn Sina and al-Biruni, the philosophy–theology confrontation, Khayyam's calendar, and al-Jazari's machines

entries.label: Ibn Sina — the summit of falsafa
entries.hint: Physician, philosopher and vizier, Ibn Sina wrote the 'Canon of Medicine' — a standard textbook in Europe and the Islamic world into the 17th century — and the 'Book of Healing', a philosophical encyclopedia whose distinction between necessary and contingent being, and whose account of the soul, shaped both later Islamic thought and Latin scholasticism.
entries.note: Ibn Sina, 'al-Qanun fi al-Tibb', 'Kitab al-Shifa'; Gutas, 'Avicenna and the Aristotelian Tradition' (2nd ed. 2014).

entries.label: Al-Biruni — the measure of the world
entries.hint: Carried to Ghazna as a captive scholar, al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and wrote 'India', the first attempt by anyone to describe another civilisation's science and religion on their own terms. He also measured the Earth's radius from a single mountain, tabulated specific gravities, and wrote a comparative chronology of the world's calendars.
entries.note: al-Biruni, 'Tahqiq ma li'l-Hind', 'al-Qanun al-Mas'udi', 'al-Athar al-Baqiya'; Kennedy's studies.

entries.label: Al-Ghazali against the philosophers
entries.hint: Al-Ghazali's 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' argued that on twenty points — the eternity of the world, God's knowledge of particulars, bodily resurrection — the Aristotelians of Islam contradicted both reason and revelation, and on three were unbelievers. The Andalusi Ibn Rushd's reply, the 'Incoherence of the Incoherence', was read more in Latin Europe than in the Muslim east.
entries.note: al-Ghazali, 'Tahafut al-Falasifa'; Ibn Rushd, 'Tahafut al-Tahafut'; the fate of falsafa (Griffel 2009; the 'decline' debate, El-Rouayheb, 'Islamic Intellectual History in the Seventeenth Century', 2015).

entries.label: Omar Khayyam — cubic equations and a calendar
entries.hint: Khayyam gave the first systematic treatment of cubic equations, solving them geometrically by intersecting conic sections, and headed the commission that produced the Jalali calendar of 1079 — a solar calendar more accurate than the Gregorian one adopted in Europe five centuries later.
entries.note: Khayyam, 'Risala fi'l-barahin ala masa'il al-jabr wa'l-muqabala'; the Jalali calendar.

entries.label: Al-Jazari's Book of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
entries.hint: Al-Jazari's treatise, written the year he died, describes fifty machines with the drawings and tolerances to build them: water-raising pumps with a true crankshaft and a double-acting piston, the elephant clock, a hand-washing automaton, and musical robots that could be reprogrammed. It is the high point of medieval mechanical engineering.
entries.note: al-Jazari, 'Kitab fi Ma'rifat al-Hiyal al-Handasiyya', trans. Hill (1974); the crankshaft and segmental gears.
keywords: Al-Jazari Book of Ingenious Mechanical Devices

entries.label: Ibn al-Athir and the historians of the catastrophe
entries.hint: Ibn al-Athir's 'Complete History' is the great narrative synthesis of the medieval Islamic world, and its account of the Mongol conquest — 'a calamity such as had not been seen before' — is the record of a civilisation watching itself attacked. Yaqut's geographical dictionary and Ibn Khallikan's biographical one belong to the same generation of great compilations.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir, 'al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh', the Mongol passages trans. Richards (2008); Yaqut, 'Mu'jam al-Buldan'; Robinson, 'Islamic Historiography' (2003).

entries.label: The Fihrist — a catalogue of everything written
entries.hint: Ibn al-Nadim, a Baghdad bookseller, compiled the 'Fihrist' — an annotated index of every book he knew to exist in Arabic, with notes on their authors, on scripts and religions, on the Greek and Indian and Persian sources. It is a snapshot of the entire intellectual production of the Islamic world at its peak.
entries.note: Ibn al-Nadim, 'al-Fihrist', trans. Dodge (1970).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The centre shifts from Iraq to Cairo and Isfahan, the Sawad finishes its collapse, and commerce keeps going through the wars

entries.label: The economic centre leaves Iraq
entries.hint: As Baghdad declined, the weight of the Islamic economy moved to Fatimid then Ayyubid Cairo — the great clearing-house of the Red Sea and Mediterranean trades — and to the Seljuk capital of Isfahan. Iraq went from the richest province of the caliphate to a contested march.
entries.note: Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society' (1967–93), on the Cairo Geniza economy; Ashtor, 'A Social and Economic History of the Near East in the Middle Ages' (1976).

entries.label: The end of the Sawad
entries.hint: The great Nahrawan canal was breached in a war in 937 and never repaired. Over the next three centuries the irrigation grid of southern Iraq decayed, the fields salted and shrank, and the population fell — so that when the Mongols came in 1258 they finished a land that was already half ruined.
entries.note: Christensen, 'The Decline of Iranshahr: Irrigation and Environment in the History of the Middle East' (1993); Adams, 'Land Behind Baghdad' (1965).

entries.label: The militarised land
entries.hint: With the iqta the dominant form of military pay, land and its revenue passed increasingly into the hands of Turkish soldiers and their households. The free village community weakened, tax pressure on the peasant rose, and the state's cash income shrank — a structural shift the later Mongol and Mamluk regimes inherited.
entries.note: Lambton, 'Continuity and Change in Medieval Persia' (1988); the iqta debate (Cahen).

entries.label: The Red Sea route and the Karimi merchants
entries.hint: The long-distance spice and luxury trade with India and the Far East shifted from the Gulf, which had run it under the Abbasids, to the Red Sea and Cairo. A wealthy guild-like body of merchants, the Karimis, came to dominate it, financing rulers and building the fortunes that Mamluk Cairo would tax.
entries.note: Fischel, 'The Spice Trade in Mamluk Egypt', JESHO (1958); the shift from the Gulf (see the Gulf folios).

entries.label: Commerce through the Crusades
entries.hint: For two centuries Italian merchant colonies in the crusader ports and in Alexandria carried European silver and cloth east and Asian spices, sugar, cotton and glass west. Popes forbade the trade in war material; it went on regardless. The Frankish states were as much a commercial interface as a battlefront.
entries.note: the Genoese and Venetian colonies (Jacoby); the papal embargoes and their evasion.

entries.label: Papermaking crosses to the Mediterranean
entries.loc: Damascus, Fustat; then Fez and Xativa
entries.hint: The paper industry spread west from Iraq — to Syria and Egypt, then across North Africa to Fez, and to Muslim Spain, where the mills of Xativa were exporting to Christian Europe by the 12th century. The last stop before Italy took up the craft in the 1270s.
entries.note: Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001), chs. 3–4; the Xativa (Játiva) mills. Cross-references the Al-Andalus folios.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The programmable automaton, the windmill, the trebuchet, and the first research observatory

entries.label: The crankshaft and the reciprocating pump
entries.hint: Al-Jazari's water-raising machine used a true crankshaft to convert the rotation of a water-wheel into the back-and-forth of a double-acting suction pump — the crank-connecting-rod mechanism and the reciprocating piston pump, both appearing in a working design centuries before their European use.
entries.note: al-Jazari (1206), trans. Hill (1974); Hill, 'A History of Engineering in Classical and Medieval Times' (1984).

entries.label: The Persian windmill
entries.hint: The earliest windmills for which there is clear evidence were vertical-axis machines on the windy plains of eastern Iran, walled to catch the seasonal 'wind of 120 days' and used to grind grain and pump water. Some at Nashtifan are still turning.
entries.note: the Sistan/Nishtifan windmills; al-Mas'udi's 10th-century notice; Hill (1984).

entries.label: The counterweight trebuchet and the citadel
entries.loc: the siege warfare of Syria and the Jazira
entries.hint: The counterweight trebuchet — heavier, more accurate and longer-ranged than the older traction machine — spread through the Islamic world in the century of the Crusades, and rulers answered it by rebuilding their cities' citadels (Aleppo, Cairo, Damascus) on a massive new scale. Fortification and artillery escalated together.
entries.note: Chevedden, 'The Invention of the Counterweight Trebuchet', DOP (2000); the Ayyubid citadels.

entries.label: The Maragha observatory
entries.hint: The year after Baghdad fell, Hulagu founded for Nasir al-Din al-Tusi an observatory at Maragha with a library, a staff of astronomers from across Asia, and large mural instruments. It was the first true scientific research institution of its kind, and its planetary models fed, through unclear channels, into Copernicus.
entries.note: Sayili, 'The Observatory in Islam' (1960); the 'Tusi couple' and the Maragha school (Saliba, 'Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance', 2007). A bridge past 1258.

entries.label: Distillation, glass and the perfume trade
entries.hint: The alembic still, refined by the Islamic chemists, supported industries in rosewater, essential oils and medicinal spirits, traded from Shiraz and Damascus across the region and into Europe. Syrian and Iraqi glassmakers, meanwhile, developed enamelled and gilded wares that the Mongol advance would scatter to Egypt.
entries.note: the alembic and the perfume industry (al-Kindi's 'Book of the Chemistry of Perfume'); enamelled glass (Carboni, 'Glass from Islamic Lands', 2001).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Turks into the heartland, the Crusades as two-way contact, the sciences pass to Latin Europe, and the Mongol rupture

entries.label: The Turkish migration into the Middle East
entries.loc: from the steppe into Iran, Iraq, Anatolia
entries.hint: The Seljuk conquest brought not just a ruling house but the Oghuz Turkish tribes behind it, moving their flocks into the settled lands. After Manzikert (1071) they poured into Anatolia and stayed; within two centuries the plateau that had been Greek for a thousand years was Turkish and Muslim.
entries.note: the Turkification of Anatolia (Vryonis, 'The Decline of Medieval Hellenism in Asia Minor', 1971; Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire', 2015).

entries.label: The Crusades as contact
entries.hint: Two centuries of Franks living in Syria and Palestine produced real exchange: crusader castle-building learned from and taught Muslim engineers; sugar-cane cultivation, learned in the Levant, followed the crusaders home; and both sides wrote ethnography of the other — Usama ibn Munqidh's bemused 'Book of Contemplation', William of Tyre's history.
entries.note: Usama ibn Munqidh, 'Kitab al-I'tibar' (trans. Cobb, 'The Book of Contemplation', 2008); the transmission of sugar and fortification technique.

entries.label: The sciences pass to Latin Europe
entries.hint: Just as al-Ghazali was checking the prestige of philosophy in the east, translators in Toledo and Sicily were turning the Arabic corpus — Ibn Sina's Canon, al-Khwarizmi's arithmetic and algebra, Ibn Rushd's Aristotle commentaries, Ptolemy via Arabic — into Latin. The medieval Islamic intellectual inheritance largely reached the modern world through this door.
entries.note: Burnett, 'The Introduction of Arabic Learning into England' and the Toledo translators; Fibonacci's 'Liber Abaci' (1202) for the numerals. Cross-references the Al-Andalus folios.

entries.label: The overland route and the Central Asian cities
entries.hint: Before the Mongols, the great cities of Khurasan and Transoxiana were among the largest and richest in the Islamic world, hubs of the overland trade in silk, paper, slaves and horses and centres of learning that produced al-Biruni, al-Bukhari and Ibn Sina. The 1219–21 conquest ended that world in two years.
entries.note: the pre-Mongol prosperity of Khurasan (Bulliet, 'The Patricians of Nishapur', 1972); the scale of the destruction (Juvayni; Ibn al-Athir).

entries.label: The scholars flee the Mongols
entries.loc: from Iran and Iraq to Cairo, Damascus and Delhi
entries.hint: The Mongol conquest drove a generation of scholars, craftsmen and Sufis west and east — to Mamluk Cairo, which became the new centre of Sunni learning, and to the Delhi Sultanate, which its refugee talent helped turn into a major Islamic state. Catastrophe redistributed the civilisation.
entries.note: the refugee scholars in Mamluk Cairo (Berkey, 'The Transmission of Knowledge in Medieval Cairo', 1992); the Persianate turn of Delhi (Kumar).

entries.label: The Mongols and the wider world
entries.loc: Karakorum; the courts of Europe and Cairo
entries.hint: As the Mongols advanced, popes and kings sent friars to their court (Carpini, Rubruck) hoping for an ally against Islam, and Muslim rulers weighed submission against resistance. The Ilkhanate that took Iran and Iraq would spend decades courting the Latin west against the Mamluks — an alliance that never quite happened.
entries.note: John of Plano Carpini and William of Rubruck's reports; Jackson, 'The Mongols and the West' (2005).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Shi'i century, the Seljuk restoration, the Crusades, the rise of the Mamluks, and the Mongol end

entries.label: The Shi'i century
entries.hint: For a hundred years the major powers of the Islamic world were Shia: the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt and the Hijaz, the Buyids in Iraq and western Iran, the Hamdanids in Syria, the Qarmatians in eastern Arabia. The Sunni Abbasid caliph was a protected relic in the middle of it.
entries.note: the 'Shi'i century' (Canard; Daftary 2007); the Fatimid–Buyid relationship.

entries.label: The Seljuk restoration
entries.hint: Tughril's entry into Baghdad reversed the Shi'i century: a Sunni Turkic power now stood behind the caliph, and the sultanate became the permanent secular counterpart to the caliphal office. Turkic military dominance of the Islamic heartlands, begun at Samarra, was now the settled order.
entries.note: Peacock, 'The Great Seljuk Empire' (2015); the sultanate as an institution.

entries.label: The Crusades
entries.hint: The Latin west's two-century attempt to hold Jerusalem and a strip of the Syrian coast was, for the Islamic world, a chronic frontier war rather than an existential threat — but it forged the careers of Nur al-Din and Saladin, hardened the ideology of jihad, and left a long memory that modern politics revived.
entries.note: Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives' (1999); the modern afterlife of the memory.

entries.label: The Ayyubids and the Mamluk coup
entries.hint: Saladin abolished the Fatimid caliphate in 1171 and built an Ayyubid confederation over Egypt and Syria. In 1250 the Turkish slave-soldiers of the Egyptian army killed the last Ayyubid and took power themselves — the Mamluk Sultanate, the state that would halt the Mongols and outlast the Crusades.
entries.note: the Mamluk seizure of power (Irwin, 'The Middle East in the Middle Ages', 1986); Ayn Jalut (1260).

entries.label: The Mongol cataclysm
entries.hint: In forty years the Mongols destroyed Khwarazm, sacked Baghdad and ended the caliphate, and set up the Ilkhanate over Iran and Iraq. The advance was finally checked by the Mamluks at Ayn Jalut in 1260. The eastern Islamic world was left depopulated in places, ruled by pagans, and permanently reoriented.
entries.note: Morgan, 'The Mongols' (2nd ed. 2007); Jackson, 'The Mongols and the Islamic World' (2017); Ayn Jalut as the limit.

entries.label: The end of the institutional caliphate
entries.loc: Baghdad; then a shadow line at Cairo from 1261
entries.hint: The killing of al-Musta'sim ended the caliphate as a functioning institution. In 1261 the Mamluks installed an Abbasid refugee in Cairo as a titular caliph, kept as a source of legitimacy with no power at all — a shadow line that lasted until the Ottomans in 1517, and a claim the Ottoman sultans then took up themselves.
entries.note: the Cairo Abbasid caliphate (Holt, 'Some Observations on the Abbasid Caliphate of Cairo', BSOAS 1984); the later Ottoman claim as coda.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The scholar's career, the Sufi lodge, the fida'i, the women traditionists, and the human toll of the conquest

entries.label: The making of the ulama class
entries.loc: the madrasas of Baghdad, Nishapur, Damascus
entries.hint: The madrasa, the endowed stipend, the licence to transmit (ijaza) and the years of travel in search of teachers turned the scholars into a professional estate — self-reproducing through family and marriage, funded largely by waqf, and increasingly tied to the state that paid it and the rulers it legitimated.
entries.note: Makdisi, 'The Rise of Colleges' (1981); Chamberlain, 'Knowledge and Social Practice in Medieval Damascus' (1994).

entries.label: The women traditionists of Damascus and Baghdad
entries.hint: Women held a recognised place in the transmission of hadith: the long-lived, respected female authority whose short chain of transmitters made her isnad valuable, so that male scholars sought her out for a licence. Their names run through the transmission histories of al-Bukhari's Sahih in this period.
entries.note: Sayeed, 'Women and the Transmission of Religious Knowledge in Islam' (2013); the female isnads of the Damascus Sahih transmission.

entries.label: The fida'i and the legend of the Assassins
entries.hint: The Nizari 'devotees' who carried out the killings were the objects, in Crusader and Sunni polemic alike, of a lurid legend — a secret garden, a drugged paradise, the word 'assassin' from 'hashish'. The reality was a besieged minority using targeted killing because it had no army, and a discipline the sources on all sides found unnerving.
entries.note: Daftary, 'The Assassin Legends: Myths of the Ismailis' (1994); Marco Polo's version as the crystallised legend.

entries.label: The mamluk household
entries.hint: By this period the enslaved-soldier household was the basic unit of Islamic politics: a commander bought and raised boys who became his loyal officers and, on his death, his faction. It gave men of servile origin routes to the highest power — and in Egypt in 1250 the mamluks stopped serving masters and became the state.
entries.note: the mamluk institution (Ayalon's studies; Amitai, 'Holy War and Rapprochement', 2013 for the later period).

entries.label: The beloved and the jurist — a continuing tension
entries.hint: The love of a beautiful youth remained a central theme of Persian and Arabic poetry — Khayyam, the Sufi lyric, the court panegyric — and a recognised feature of elite male life, even as the jurists held the act of liwat to be a capital crime and the Sufis debated whether gazing at a beautiful face was worship or sin. Prescription and practice stayed far apart.
entries.note: El-Rouayheb, 'Before Homosexuality in the Arab-Islamic World, 1500–1800' (2005) on the later continuity; the Sufi 'gazing' (nazar) debate. Cross-references the ghulam and mukhannath entries.

entries.label: The human toll of the Mongol conquest
entries.hint: The sources give city death-tolls in the hundreds of thousands or more — figures modern historians cut but do not dismiss. Whatever the numbers, the conquest killed a large share of the urban population of Khurasan and Iraq, scattered the survivors, and broke the demographic and agricultural base of the eastern Islamic world for a century.
entries.note: the casualty debate (Morgan, 'The Mongols', 2007; Petrushevsky in the Cambridge History of Iran vol. 5); the archaeological and settlement evidence.
